claims.text: Aging an fcc Fe-Co-Ni-Ti alloy can cause controlled nanoscale phase decomposition while retaining an fcc matrix.
The proposed decomposition produces a ferromagnetic fcc matrix containing a Ti-rich B2 or L12 secondary phase.
A magnetically hard or antiferromagnetically coupled secondary phase will act as a domain-wall-pinning phase.
Secondary-phase pinning will overcome the orbital-moment suppression found in single-phase fcc systems.
The initial alloy can be an as-cast, single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni-Ti alloy containing 5-15 at.% Ti.
Minor Mn or Cr additions can tune magnetic interactions in the proposed Fe-Co-Ni-Ti alloy.
Solution annealing at 1000-1100 degrees C followed by aging at 600-800 degrees C will induce spinodal decomposition or nucleation of an ordered secondary phase.
Aging for 10-100 hours at 600-800 degrees C can produce precipitates 10-50 nm in size at a volume fraction of 5-15%.
The secondary precipitates will be coherent or semi-coherent with the fcc matrix.
Coherent or semi-coherent precipitates create local strain fields and magnetic-exchange-coupling boundaries.
Chemical interaction between the fcc matrix and Ti-rich precipitates modifies local exchange interactions.
The proposed matrix-precipitate interaction prevents suppression of the orbital moment.
Precipitates increase the energy barrier for domain-wall motion and therefore increase coercivity.
Multiphase HEA microstructures can have magnetic properties influenced by composition and the length scale of phase decomposition.
The aged Fe-Co-Ni-Ti alloy will exhibit coercivity exceeding 100 Oe.
Aging will slightly reduce saturation magnetization relative to the corresponding single-phase state.
The Curie temperature will remain significantly above room temperature because the fcc matrix is ferromagnetic and the precipitates are stable at high temperature.
An unaged single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni-Ti alloy typically has coercivity below 20 Oe because of orbital-moment suppression and insufficient domain-wall pinning.
Effective coercivity enhancement requires coherent or semi-coherent secondary phases smaller than 100 nm, whereas incoherent precipitates larger than 200 nm may reduce coercivity.
Ti must be sufficiently concentrated to drive phase separation but not so concentrated that it destabilizes the fcc matrix.
